blocks.en: In the tug-of-war the two teams pull on the rope with the same force. The rope does not move, yet nobody is resting: both teams keep pulling all the time.

items.en: This is dynamic equilibrium: the forward and the reverse changes go on at the same rate, so nothing seems to change.
In a reversible reaction such as N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ the rate at which ammonia forms equals the rate at which it breaks up again, so the amounts of N₂, H₂ and NH₃ stay constant.

Equilibrium is reached only in a closed system; if one team pulls harder (a factor changes), the rope moves until a new balance is found, just as a reaction shifts when temperature, pressure or concentration is changed.

blocks.en: The production of ammonia: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), the reaction gives out heat (exothermic) and 4 moles of gas make 2 moles of gas.

rows: The forward reaction is exothermic, so a lower temperature gives more ammonia, but a very low temperature makes it too slow; about 450 °C is the compromise.
4 moles of gas become 2 moles, so a higher pressure (about 200 atmospheres) moves the equilibrium to the right and gives more ammonia.
More nitrogen or hydrogen, or taking the ammonia away as it forms, shifts the equilibrium to the right.
Iron makes the equilibrium be reached faster, but it does not change the amount of ammonia at equilibrium.

blocks.en: So all four affect the production of ammonia, but a catalyst affects only how fast it is made, not how much.

items.en: What happens: the mixture fizzes, a gas is formed and the balloon swells up and stands on the bottle.
The reaction: citric acid (in lemon juice) + sodium hydrogencarbonate (baking soda) → sodium citrate + water + carbon dioxide gas.
In general: acid + hydrogencarbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide fills the balloon.
Proof: the gas puts out a burning splint and turns lime water milky.

blocks.en: Method for the soil: mix a spoon of soil with some distilled water, let it settle, dip a strip of pH paper in the clear water and compare the colour with the chart. Red or orange means acidic (pH below 7), green means neutral (7), blue or purple means basic (above 7). Most garden soils are close to neutral (pH 6 to 8).
An alkyl group is an alkane that has lost one hydrogen atom; its name is the alkane's name with -ane changed to -yl (butane to butyl, hexane to hexyl).
Members of a homologous series differ by one CH₂ group, so the next member has one more carbon and two more hydrogens.

blocks.en: b. Organic compounds and their uses

items.en: Methane, propane, butane and petrol: fuels.
Ethanol: solvent, disinfectant, fuel additive. Ethanoic (acetic) acid: vinegar.
Polythene and PVC: plastic bags and pipes. Glucose, sucrose, starch: food. Soap and detergents: cleaning.
Medicines such as aspirin and paracetamol; dyes, perfumes and fabrics such as nylon and polyester.

blocks.en: c. For the class discussion

Organic compounds are the basis of life (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, DNA) and of fuels, plastics, medicines and fibres. Carbon can form long chains and rings, and so makes millions of compounds. Misuse of plastics and fuels also harms the environment, so they must be used carefully.

work.starts: Making models of first five alkanes and alkenes

items.en: Alkanes: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Alkenes: CₙH₂ₙ (the first alkene has two carbons, so ethene is the first alkene).
Use black beads for carbon and white beads for hydrogen. Join the two carbons of an alkene with two sticks (or springs) to show the double bond; every other bond is one stick.
Show in class that an alkane carbon has four single bonds and an alkene carbon in C=C has two single bonds and one double bond.

blocks.en: The alkene adds bromine across the double bond (an addition reaction): C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂ (1,2-dibromoethane, colourless). This decolourising of bromine is the test for unsaturation.

work.starts: Relative Solubility in Water of Starch and Sugar

rows: What you see after stirring for 5 minutes
The sugar dissolves completely: a clear solution.
The starch does not dissolve: the water stays cloudy and white starch settles at the bottom.

items.en: 1. Yes, the two beakers can be told apart by solubility: sugar is soluble in water, starch is not (it only forms a cloudy suspension).
2. The soluble compound is sugar. Sugars are small molecules (glucose, sucrose) that mix with water; starch is a very large polysaccharide made of thousands of glucose units, too big to dissolve.

blocks.en: Yes, the normal and the denatured protein can be told apart: heating breaks the weak bonds that hold the long protein chains in their special shape, so the chains unfold and stick together (the white turns solid and opaque). This change cannot be undone. Strong acids, alcohol and heavy metals also denature proteins.

2. Why agricultural and nutritional sciences are vital

items.en: Agricultural science finds ways to grow more and better food (seeds, fertilisers, protection from pests and disease) for a growing population.
Nutritional science tells what and how much to eat for health, and how to prevent malnutrition and diseases such as anaemia, obesity and diabetes.
Together they make sure that enough safe, nourishing food reaches everyone.

1. The greenhouse effect and global warming: what to show

items.en: Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth. The Earth gives out heat as infrared radiation.
Greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour) trap part of this heat, as the glass of a greenhouse does; a little of this keeps the Earth warm.
Burning fuels, cutting forests and farming add more greenhouse gases, so the Earth warms more: ice melts, seas rise and weather becomes more extreme.
A simple model: put a thermometer in two clear jars, one with air and one filled with carbon dioxide (vinegar and baking soda), and place both in the sun. The second jar warms more.

blocks.en: 2. Controlling the air pollution from vehicle exhaust

items.en: Fit catalytic converters, which change carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides into carbon dioxide, nitrogen and water.
Service engines regularly; use better quality fuel (low sulphur) and CNG; check the smoke of vehicles.
Use public transport, bicycles and electric vehicles; plant trees along roads.
Your report: how you measured (counting vehicles, checking smoke), results and which of these steps would help most.

work.starts: Ice Floats on the Surface of Water

items.en: iv. The ice floats because ice is less dense than liquid water (about 0.92 g per cm³ against 1.00 g per cm³). In ice the water molecules are held by hydrogen bonds in an open, six-sided pattern with gaps, so the same mass takes about 9% more space.
v. Other substances that float on water: oil, petrol, wood, cork, a plastic bottle, a leaf, a foam sheet.

blocks.en: Set up as in the book: two beakers of water, calcium chloride in one, carbon dioxide blown through both with a straw.

SpaceBook note on the result: the usual test for carbon dioxide uses lime water (calcium hydroxide): Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ (white, milky) + H₂O. Plain calcium chloride solution is not basic, so carbon dioxide does not turn it milky; it stays clear. If your beaker with calcium chloride stays clear, that is the correct chemistry: use lime water to see the milkiness.

work.starts: In which beaker water turns milky

items.en: v. The beaker that turns milky is the one that holds a basic calcium compound, for example lime water: carbon dioxide makes white calcium carbonate that does not dissolve. Beaker with only water stays clear (it just becomes slightly acidic, carbonic acid).

vi. Other salts and bases that turn milky on passing CO₂: barium hydroxide solution (barium carbonate) and strontium hydroxide; with more CO₂ the milkiness clears again, as the carbonate changes to soluble hydrogencarbonate.
Note: calcium chloride itself does not make the water milky (see the note under Activity 15.3).
iv. After 10 minutes, if the water had suspended dirt, the water becomes clear: a jelly-like deposit settles at the bottom.

v. Why: alum dissolves and its aluminium ions form flakes of aluminium hydroxide, which trap the suspended particles and carry them to the bottom (coagulation and sedimentation). That is why alum (phitkari) is used to clear muddy water.
In clear water nothing much is seen except that the water becomes very slightly cloudy at first and the alum solution is slightly acidic.

blocks.en: Ways to remove them and to prevent water contamination

items.en: Boil drinking water for at least one minute; or treat it with chlorine or purifying tablets.
Filter and settle muddy water (cloth, sand filter, alum) before treating it.
Keep sewage away from drinking water: covered drains, protected wells and pipes, proper toilets.
Cover stored water, use a clean cup with a handle, and wash hands with soap before eating and after the toilet.
Do not throw waste, factory water or pesticides into rivers, canals and ponds.

rows: Fertilisers add nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium to the soil, so crops give a much larger yield.
Too much fertiliser washes into rivers and lakes (eutrophication) and harms fish and water plants.
Without them the land would not feed the growing population, and more forest would be cleared for farms.
Nitrate in drinking water is harmful, especially for babies; fertilisers also add greenhouse gases (nitrous oxide).
They act quickly, are easy to store and apply, and their composition is known.
They cost money and make farmers depend on factories; they do not improve the soil's structure, as manure and compost do.
Used in the right amount and at the right time, losses are small.
Better solutions together: manure, crop rotation with beans, using less food waste and less meat, and efficient use of fertiliser.

blocks.en: A balanced conclusion: artificial fertilisers are needed to feed the world, but 'best solution' is too strong; they work best together with careful use and natural methods.

blocks.en: Each fertiliser has its own use because crops and soils need different nutrients, and because of cost, how easy it is to make, how much nutrient there is per rupee and how it reaches the farmer. Many are made like this: urea from ammonia and carbon dioxide; ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen (Haber process); phosphate fertilisers from rock phosphate with acid.
